lesson.title: One Equation for Every First-Order Transient
lesson.summary: Charging, discharging, energizing, and de-energizing all turn out to be the same underlying pattern, a variable moving exponentially from its initial value to its final value at a rate set by the circuit's time constant.
lesson.body:
Look back at the last four transients: a capacitor charging toward a source, a capacitor discharging toward zero, an inductor's current climbing toward its final value, and an inductor's current decaying away. Each one was solved with its own formula, and each one, once you strip away the specific labels, was doing exactly the same thing: starting at one value, ending at another, and getting from one to the other along an exponential curve at a rate set by the time constant. That is not a coincidence, it is because every one of these circuits is described by the same first-order differential equation, just with different variables plugged in.

That common pattern can be written as a single general formula that covers all four cases at once: x(t) = x_final + (x_initial - x_final)*e^(-t/tau), where x can stand for a capacitor voltage, an inductor current, or in fact any voltage or current anywhere in a first-order circuit. x_initial is the value of that quantity right at the moment the transient begins, x_final is the value it is heading toward as t goes to infinity, and tau is RC for a capacitive circuit or L/R for an inductive one. Everything about the transient's timeline, direction, and shape is packed into just those three numbers.

The four earlier formulas are simply this equation with specific values dropped in. RC charging had x_initial = 0 and x_final = Vs, which turns the general formula into Vs + (0 - Vs)*e^(-t/RC) = Vs*(1 - e^(-t/RC)), matching what was derived before. RC discharging had x_initial = V0 and x_final = 0, giving 0 + (V0 - 0)*e^(-t/RC) = V0*e^(-t/RC). The RL cases work the same way with current in place of voltage and L/R in place of RC. None of those earlier derivations were really separate results, they were the same equation wearing different clothes.

The real payoff of the general formula is that you no longer have to remember four separate cases, you just need to find three numbers using simple DC reasoning: the value right before the change, the value the circuit is settling toward, and the time constant. For example, suppose a capacitor sitting at v(0) = 3 V is suddenly connected into a new circuit that will eventually charge it to v(infinity) = 15 V, with a time constant tau = 2 ms. To find the voltage at t = 4 ms, which is two time constants, apply the formula directly: v(4ms) = 15 + (3 - 15)*e^(-4/2) = 15 + (-12)*e^-2 = 15 - 12*0.1353 = 15 - 1.624 = 13.38 V.

This is the real skill first-order circuit analysis is building toward. At steady state, a capacitor behaves like an open circuit and an inductor behaves like a short circuit, which lets you find x_initial and x_final with basic Ohm's law reasoning rather than calculus, and tau comes straight from R and C or L, exactly as in the time constant discussion. Once those three quantities are in hand, the general exponential formula writes the entire time response of the circuit for you.
